analysis.one_liner: Requires baby food and formula makers to test for lead, arsenic, and dangerous germs and report contamination.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 5 cosponsors on March 27, 2025, has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no markup, vote, or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The INFANTS Act would require companies that make baby food and infant formula to test their products for toxic heavy metals like lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury every quarter, keep records of the results, and hand those records to the FDA. Formula makers would have to tell the FDA within 24 hours whenever testing finds dangerous pathogens like Salmonella or Listeria, destroy the affected product, and run ongoing monitoring of their plants for Cronobacter and Salmonella. Food found to be made without following these rules would be treated as adulterated and kept off store shelves.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and babies who eat infant and toddler food gain a layer of protection against heavy metals like lead and arsenic, and against bacteria like Salmonella and Cronobacter in powdered formula — the kind of contamination that has led to recalls and shortages in recent years. State and federal food-safety regulators also gain clearer records and faster notice when pathogens are found.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents and babies eating baby food

how_it_helps.text: Requires facilities that make infant and toddler food in final form to sample and test for lead, cadmium, mercury, arsenic, and any other contaminants the FDA specifies, at least once every calendar quarter.
Treats food made at a facility that fails to comply with the testing requirements as adulterated, meaning it legally cannot be sold into interstate commerce.

Requires formula manufacturers that get a confirmed positive test for an environmental pathogen such as Listeria or Salmonella to notify the FDA within 24 hours, dispose of the affected product properly, and hand over test results and samples — tightening the current 'promptly' standard to a hard 24-hour deadline.

Requires powdered infant formula makers to run a written environmental monitoring program to verify that sanitation and hygiene controls are working where Cronobacter or Salmonella could contaminate the product — the bacterium behind the 2022 formula recalls and shortage.
Gives the FDA clearer recall authority over adulterated infant and toddler food, though the bill first requires the FDA to offer the company a chance to recall voluntarily.

analysis.who_pays: Infant formula and baby food manufacturers, who would bear the cost of quarterly accredited laboratory testing, written sampling plans, two years of recordkeeping, plant environmental monitoring, and possible recalls — costs they may pass through in prices. The FDA also takes on guidance-writing and follow-up review work.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on manufacturers and could be passed on to parents through higher prices, and smaller producers with thin margins may find quarterly accredited testing and new monitoring programs hardest to absorb. The testing requirement does not even begin until 180 days after the FDA publishes guidance, which the agency has 18 months to write, so relief would be years away.

The bill actually narrows the FDA's recall power for contaminated baby food: for infant and toddler food other than formula found adulterated by a contaminant, the FDA must first give the company an opportunity to conduct a voluntary recall before forcing one, a carve-out critics could argue lets the industry manage its own bad news.

Testing done under the bill is expressly exempted from the stricter laboratory accreditation requirements of section 422 of the food safety law, so labs only need to meet international accreditation standards rather than the program Congress set up for food testing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — parents knowing that baby food and formula are tested for lead, arsenic, and deadly bacteria, with fast FDA notification when something is found — is substantial and cheap relative to the stakes for infants, who are most vulnerable to heavy-metal and pathogen exposure. The compliance costs on manufacturers are real but modest for an industry of this size, and testing baby food for heavy metals is a standard practice many large producers already claim to run. The genuine design flaws are the slow start (up to two years before testing is required) and the voluntary-recall-first provision, which weaken the bill but do not offset its main purpose.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in March 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes of Ohio introduced the INFANTS Act on March 27, 2025, with Reps. Frank Pallone and Raja Krishnamoorthi as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds jurisdiction over food and drug safety.
Five members cosponsored the bill — four Democrats and one Republican — and no further action has been recorded: no hearings, no markup, no vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, baby food and infant formula manufacturers are better off, because no testing, monitoring, or 24-hour reporting requirements have been imposed on them. Parents and babies gain nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Baby food and formula makers, so far

industries.note: Powdered formula makers would face mandatory environmental monitoring for Cronobacter and Salmonella, a hard 24-hour deadline to report positive pathogen tests and destroy affected product, and extra recordkeeping. These requirements exist because pathogens in formula plants have previously led to recalls, a nationwide shortage, and sickened infants.

Makers of foods for children up to 24 months would have to test every product quarterly for lead, cadmium, mercury, and arsenic at accredited labs, keep records for at least two years, and provide them to the FDA on request — and food made at a noncompliant facility would be barred from sale. Heavy metals have repeatedly been found in baby food, which is why the testing requirement targets this industry specifically.

Quarterly, internationally accredited testing of every infant and toddler food would create a new steady stream of paid lab work. The bill also exempts this testing from the stricter section 422 lab accreditation program, slightly widening which labs can compete for it.

analysis.trajectory: Food-safety bills referred to Energy and Commerce rarely move on their own unless the committee leadership schedules a markup, and no hearing or markup has been set. With only five cosponsors and nine months of inaction, the likeliest path is that the bill sits in committee until the Congress ends, unless its provisions get folded into a larger food or drug safety package that does move.
